title: Reading the Room
goal: Your kid learns to notice how the people and places around them are doing. They spot the clues in faces, voices and rooms, guess the mood, check it with one kind question, match their voice and energy to it, and then do something about it, like the day they noticed you weren't okay and made dinner.
need: Everyday places: home, a café, a park, a museum
A notebook for the room reading log
Your honest answers when they check on you

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: The trap is telling them how to behave everywhere you go. Your job is to ask what they notice, let them guess, and point it out when they read a room well on their own.

plan.what: Spot the clues and guess the mood, anywhere (Steps 1 and 2).
Check, match and act with the people they live with (Steps 3 to 5).
Add it to the room reading log.

troubleshoot.a: That's how they learn. Talk about which clue fooled them, and what they could check next time.

troubleshoot.q: They notice, but don't do anything
troubleshoot.a: Start with tiny actions: a glass of water, a quieter voice, a seat saved. Thank them every time.
Remind them that one kind question beats guessing all day. They don't have to read everyone.

lesson.text: Reading the room has three parts: noticing the clues, checking what they mean, and doing something about it. Most kids stop at the first part. The ones who check and act are the ones people feel cared for by.

model.line: Something was off, even before dinner.
He and his sister made dinner.

lesson.modelNote: He didn't wait to be asked. He noticed, he checked with one question, and then he and his sister did something about it. That's reading the room all the way to the end.

steps.title: Spot the clues
steps.why: Moods leave clues everywhere: in faces, voices, bodies and in the room itself. Kids who look for clues first make better guesses.
steps.kid: Your kid watches one person or one place for a couple of minutes and names the clues they see, using the People clues and Room clues cards in the Room Reading Toolkit at the end of the guide. No guessing yet, just clues.
steps.you: Play clue detectives anywhere: a café, a park, a waiting room. Whisper your clues to each other, and keep it kind.
ask: What do you notice about how people are talking in here?
What is that person's face telling you?
steps.tip: Clues first, guesses second. Kids who jump straight to a guess often guess wrong.

levels.explore: Spot one face clue and one voice clue on someone in a book or a show.
levels.develop: List four clues about a person or a place you're in.
levels.extend: Watch a room for five minutes, and notice how the clues change.

steps.title: Guess the mood
steps.why: Clues add up to a mood: playful, serious, tired, busy, sad. Naming it is what helps them decide what to do.
steps.kid: Your kid uses the clues to guess the mood of a person or a room, and says which clues made them think so.
steps.you: Make your own guess too, then compare. When you disagree, talk about which clues each of you noticed.
ask: What mood is this room in?
Which clue made you think so?
steps.tip: Two people can read the same room differently. Comparing guesses is half the learning.

levels.explore: Pick a mood word for a person or a place, with a parent.
levels.develop: Guess the mood of three people or places, and give a clue for each.
levels.extend: Guess a mood, then notice something that would change your guess.

steps.title: Check it
steps.why: A guess is just a guess. One kind question turns it into something they know.
steps.kid: When your kid thinks someone isn't okay, they check with one short question, using the Check it card: 'Are you okay?' or 'Do you want help or space?'
steps.you: Answer honestly, even when the answer is 'No, I'm not.' That honesty is what makes checking worth it.
ask: How could you find out if your guess is right?
steps.tip: Checking isn't being nosy. A short, kind question is how good readers stop guessing.

levels.explore: Ask someone in your family, 'Are you okay?' when you notice something.
levels.develop: Check one guess a day for a week, and write what you found out.
levels.extend: Check, then ask a second question: 'Do you want help or space?'

steps.title: Match it
steps.why: Every place has its own volume, pace and mood. Matching it shows the people around you that you noticed.
steps.kid: Your kid adjusts their voice, speed and energy to the room, using the Match it card: quieter and slower in a palace or a library, louder at a game, gentle at home when someone's sick.
steps.you: Name it afterwards when they did it on their own: 'You got quieter as soon as we walked in.' Kids keep what gets noticed.
ask: What should your voice be like in here?
Is this a joking moment, or not?
steps.tip: Matching isn't faking. It's a way of showing respect for the people and the place.

levels.explore: Show a parent your palace voice, your park voice and your sick-day voice.
levels.develop: Walk into a new place, and match the volume and speed of the room.
levels.extend: Notice when a joke stops being funny for someone, and stop it yourself.

steps.title: Act on it
steps.why: The best readers don't just notice. They do one small thing about it.
steps.kid: When your kid reads that someone needs something, they act: help, give space, or include someone. They write each one in My room reading log at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Let them take over sometimes, even when you could do it yourself. Then thank them for exactly what they did.
ask: What would help them right now?
Should you help, or give them space?
steps.tip: Small acts count: a glass of water, a quieter voice, a seat saved for someone new.

levels.explore: Do one small thing for someone who looks tired or sad.
levels.develop: Act on one reading each day for a week, and log it.
levels.extend: Take over a whole job, like dinner, when someone at home needs it.

conclusion.headline: They notice how people are doing, and do something about it.
conclusion.text: Watch for the next time they lower their voice in a new place, or ask someone if they're okay, before you've said a word. That's the skill working on its own.
conclusion.celebrate: When they read someone and act on it, say exactly what you saw: 'You noticed I wasn't well, and you made dinner. That meant so much to me.'
extensions: Watch a show with the sound off, and guess each character's mood
Visit a place with different rules, like a temple, a market or a library, and read it together
Notice one person each day who might need something
Ask a grandparent which places had special rules when they were young

signs: They ask 'Are you okay?' without being prompted
They change their voice in a new place on their own
They notice when a joke has stopped being funny
makeItReal: Next time you walk into somewhere new, a museum, a restaurant or a friend's house, stop at the door together for ten seconds. Ask what they notice, then let them lead the way in.

fromHome.text: The last time I was sick, I was about to make dinner when my son asked me if I was okay. He had noticed. I said no, and he and his sister took over: they made dinner, and cleaned the kitchen after. And when we visited the National Palace in San Salvador, both kids got quieter and slowed down as soon as we walked in.
